items.prompt: What does 'base rate' mean in the context of an alert or detector?
choices: How common the event being detected actually is in the population being checked
How often the detector is wrong
The detector's true positive rate
The number of times the alert has fired this month
items.explanation: Base rate is how frequently the real event actually occurs among everything being checked -- a fact about the world, not about the detector itself. It's what got ignored at 3am in L1.
items.reference:
🌍 base rate: how common the real event is, in the world
🎯 not a property of the detector at all

Why: The same detector can have wildly different real-world trustworthiness depending only on how rare its target event is.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, what was the base rate of a real incident among the checks the detector evaluated?
items.explanation: L1 states real incidents happen in about 2% of the windows the detector evaluates -- 20 out of every 1,000 checks.
items.reference:
🌍 base rate: how common the real event is, in the world
🎯 not a property of the detector at all

Why: The same detector can have wildly different real-world trustworthiness depending only on how rare its target event is.

items.prompt: A rare disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. What is the base rate of that disease, as a percentage?
items.explanation: 1 in 10,000 is 1/10,000 = 0.0001 = 0.01%. Base rate is just the real-world frequency expressed as a fraction or percentage.
items.reference:
🌍 base rate: how common the real event is, in the world
🎯 not a property of the detector at all

Why: The same detector can have wildly different real-world trustworthiness depending only on how rare its target event is.

items.prompt: Out of 1,000 checks in L1's scenario, how many total alerts fired (real plus false)?
items.explanation: 19 true positives (95% of 20 real incidents) plus 49 false positives (5% of 980 non-incidents) = 68 total alerts fired.
items.reference:

Why: Precision is real alerts divided by total alerts, not divided by real incidents.

items.prompt: Of the 68 total alerts that fired in L1's scenario, roughly what fraction were real incidents?
choices: About 28%
About 95%
About 68%
About 5%
items.explanation: 19 real alerts out of 68 total fired alerts is about 28% -- the precision of the alert, distinct from its 95% true positive rate.
items.reference:
Real incidents (20)19 caught, 1 missed
Not real (980)49 false alarms, 931 quiet
Total fired68 -- only 19 real (28%)

Why: Precision is real alerts divided by total alerts, not divided by real incidents.

items.prompt: Two metrics move together closely. What does that correlation, by itself, tell you about causation?
choices: Nothing definitive -- it's consistent with one causing the other, a shared cause, reverse causation, or coincidence
It proves the first metric causes the second
It proves the second metric causes the first
It proves there's no causal relationship at all
items.explanation: A correlation is consistent with several different underlying explanations. It doesn't distinguish between them on its own -- that takes further investigation.
items.reference:
🔗 correlation: two things move together
❓ causation: one thing brings about the other

Why: A correlation coefficient can't distinguish a confound, reverse causation, coincidence, or a real causal link -- all look the same as a number.

items.prompt: Which best defines 'causation' as distinct from 'correlation'?
choices: One thing actually brings about the other through a real mechanism, not just moving together statistically
Two quantities that happen to have similar values
Any relationship strong enough to be statistically significant
Two quantities that trend in the same direction over time
items.explanation: Causation requires an actual mechanism connecting cause to effect -- a stronger, harder-to-establish claim than 'these two numbers move together.'
items.reference:
🔗 correlation: two things move together
❓ causation: one thing brings about the other

Why: A correlation coefficient can't distinguish a confound, reverse causation, coincidence, or a real causal link -- all look the same as a number.

items.prompt: What is a 'confound'?
choices: A third factor that independently drives both of two correlated quantities
A detector's false positive rate
The formal term for a coincidental correlation
A correlation that has been statistically proven causal
items.explanation: A confound is a hidden third variable that causes both measured quantities to move together, creating the appearance of a direct link between them where none exists.
items.reference:
🔥 fire size drives both trucks dispatched and damage
🚒 trucks and damage correlate, but neither causes the other

Why: The fix for a confound is identifying and controlling for the shared cause, not looking for a stronger correlation.

items.prompt: Fires that get more fire trucks dispatched also tend to have more property damage. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: A confound -- bigger fires independently cause both more trucks dispatched and more damage
Dispatching more trucks causes more damage
More damage causes trucks to be dispatched after the fact
Pure coincidence with no explanation
items.explanation: Fire size is the confound: bigger fires get more trucks dispatched (a reasonable response) and independently cause more damage, without truck count driving damage at all.
items.reference:
🔥 fire size drives both trucks dispatched and damage
🚒 trucks and damage correlate, but neither causes the other

Why: The fix for a confound is identifying and controlling for the shared cause, not looking for a stronger correlation.

items.prompt: What does 'true positive rate' measure?
choices: Of the cases where the event is real, the fraction the detector correctly flags
Of the cases where the detector fires, the fraction that are real
Of all cases checked, the fraction where the detector fires
The overall percentage of the time the detector is correct, real or not
items.explanation: True positive rate (sensitivity) is conditioned on the event being real -- it says nothing about what happens when the detector fires on a rare event, which is precision's job.
items.reference:
✅ true positive rate: given it's real, how often caught
📉 precision: given it fired, how often real

Why: These are different conditional probabilities -- mixing them up is exactly the base rate fallacy.

items.prompt: What does 'false positive rate' measure?
choices: Of the cases where the event is NOT real, the fraction the detector incorrectly flags anyway
Of the cases where the detector fires, the fraction that turn out to be false
The total count of false alarms in a given period
The fraction of real events the detector misses
items.explanation: False positive rate is conditioned on the event NOT being real -- how often the detector cries wolf when there's genuinely nothing there.
items.reference:
✅ true positive rate: given it's real, how often caught
📉 precision: given it fired, how often real

Why: These are different conditional probabilities -- mixing them up is exactly the base rate fallacy.

items.prompt: Why did the on-call team get fooled by a '95% accurate' alert in L1, even though the detector wasn't lying?
choices: They read the detector's true positive rate as if it were the alert's precision, without accounting for how rare the real event is
The detector's true positive rate was actually much lower than 95%
The escalation policy paged too many people
The false positive rate was reported incorrectly
items.explanation: The 95% figure was true and honestly reported -- it just answered a different question (how good is the detector when tested against a known real case) than the one the team needed (how trustworthy is this specific firing).
items.reference:
🚨 3am page: '95% accurate' detector, wrong
📉 real precision at a 2% base rate: 28%

Why: No number was false -- 'accuracy' and 'trustworthy when it fires' are simply different questions.

items.prompt: What would have told the on-call team, before 3am, that the alert was less trustworthy than '95% accurate' suggested?
choices: Computing precision using the event's actual base rate, not just quoting the detector's true positive rate
Waiting for a second alert to confirm the first
Increasing the escalation policy's page threshold
Nothing -- there was no way to know in advance
items.explanation: The base rate (2%) combined with both error rates was enough to compute precision (28%) in advance, without needing to wait and see -- the information was already available, just not looked at.
items.reference:
🚨 3am page: '95% accurate' detector, wrong
📉 real precision at a 2% base rate: 28%

Why: No number was false -- 'accuracy' and 'trustworthy when it fires' are simply different questions.

choices: Team size is a plausible confound -- it independently drives both channel count and feature output
The claim is airtight -- more channels genuinely enable faster shipping
This must be reverse causation -- shipping features causes more channels
This must be pure coincidence, unrelated to team structure
items.explanation: Team size fits the confound pattern well: bigger teams naturally create more channels and independently ship more features, without channel count driving either.

items.prompt: What is the correct fix for a suspected confound, as opposed to a suspected coincidence or reverse causation?
choices: Identify the shared cause and check whether the relationship survives once it's held roughly constant
Check which variable changed first in time
Ask whether anyone can describe a plausible mechanism connecting the two
Collect a larger sample size to strengthen the correlation

items.prompt: A city with more police officers per capita has a higher crime rate. Someone concludes 'hiring more police increases crime.' What's the likely flaw?
choices: Reverse causation -- high crime likely led the city to hire more police, not the other way around
This is a confound -- some third factor drives both independently
This is airtight causal evidence that police presence increases crime
This is pure coincidence with no explanation available
items.explanation: The more plausible causal arrow runs backward: cities respond to high crime by hiring more police, rather than police presence causing crime.
items.reference:
↩️ reverse causation: the arrow points the other way
🕰️ fix: check which variable changed first

Why: A correlation coefficient has no direction built in -- 'A correlates with B' never says which one, if either, came first.

items.prompt: What's the fix for checking whether a correlation is actually reverse causation?
choices: Check the timeline -- which variable changed first, historically
Collect a larger sample size
Look for a third variable that could explain both
Ask whether the correlation coefficient is statistically significant
items.explanation: Reverse causation is specifically about which direction the causal arrow points -- checking which change happened first in time is the direct way to test that.
items.reference:
↩️ reverse causation: the arrow points the other way
🕰️ fix: check which variable changed first

Why: A correlation coefficient has no direction built in -- 'A correlates with B' never says which one, if either, came first.

items.prompt: The number of Nicolas Cage films released in a year tracks pool drowning deaths that year, closely, for a decade. What's the best explanation?
choices: Coincidence -- no plausible mechanism connects the two, and enough pairs of unrelated series will eventually correlate by chance
A confound -- some hidden factor drives both
Reverse causation -- drownings somehow affect film releases
A genuine, previously unknown causal link worth investigating further
items.explanation: With no plausible mechanism in either direction, and given how many pairs of unrelated time series exist, some will correlate strongly purely by chance -- this is the textbook spurious-correlation-by-coincidence case.
items.reference:
🎲 coincidence: no causal link at all
🧭 fix: ask for a plausible mechanism -- if none exists, that's the tell

Why: Enough pairs of unrelated series exist that some will correlate strongly by pure chance -- that's a statistical certainty, not a mystery.

items.prompt: What question best distinguishes a coincidental correlation from a real causal one?
choices: Can anyone describe, concretely, how A would physically or economically cause B?
Is the correlation coefficient above 0.9?
Has the correlation held for more than five years?
Do both variables increase over time?
items.explanation: Asking for a concrete, describable mechanism is the direct test -- a high coefficient or a long time span doesn't distinguish coincidence from causation, since a coincidental pattern can also be strong and long-lasting.
items.reference:
🎲 coincidence: no causal link at all
🧭 fix: ask for a plausible mechanism -- if none exists, that's the tell

Why: Enough pairs of unrelated series exist that some will correlate strongly by pure chance -- that's a statistical certainty, not a mystery.

items.prompt: Why does 'enough pairs of unrelated time series exist that some will correlate by chance' matter when evaluating a surprising correlation you found?
choices: Because if you searched many pairs of variables, finding one strong correlation among them is expected by chance alone, not necessarily meaningful
Because it proves every correlation found this way must be a confound
Because it means correlation coefficients are unreliable in general
Because it means the sample size was too small
items.explanation: If many pairs are compared, at least a few strong-looking correlations are statistically expected to turn up purely by chance -- the surprising find isn't automatically evidence of a real relationship just because it's strong.
items.reference:

🧭 fix: ask for a plausible mechanism -- if none exists, that's the tell

items.explanation: 5% of 980 non-incidents = 49 false alarms -- the false positive rate applied to the (much larger) pool of non-events.
items.reference:

Precision19 / 68 ≈ 28%

Why: The false positive rate applies to the much larger pool of non-events, which is why it dominates precision at a low base rate.

items.prompt: In the plain-text Bayes formula from L2 (P(real given alert fires)), what goes in the denominator?
choices: base_rate * true_positive_rate + (1 - base_rate) * false_positive_rate -- the total probability the alert fires at all
Just the true_positive_rate
Just the base_rate
1 minus the false_positive_rate
items.explanation: The denominator is the total probability the alert fires, from any cause -- real incidents caught, plus non-incidents falsely flagged. The numerator (just the real-and-fired term) divided by that total gives precision.
items.reference:
Real (20)19 caught, 1 missed
Not real (980)49 false alarms, 931 quiet
Precision19 / 68 ≈ 28%

Why: The false positive rate applies to the much larger pool of non-events, which is why it dominates precision at a low base rate.

items.prompt: What, precisely, is the 'base rate fallacy'?
choices: Ignoring how rare an event actually is and over-trusting a positive signal, effectively confusing true positive rate with precision
Believing rare events never happen at all
Assuming a detector's false positive rate is always zero
Using percentages instead of raw counts when reasoning about probability
items.explanation: The base rate fallacy is specifically about neglecting the real-world frequency of the event and treating a detector's own accuracy figure (usually its true positive rate) as if it directly told you the signal's trustworthiness.
items.reference:
🧮 base rate fallacy: ignoring how rare the event is
🔀 confusing true positive rate with precision

Why: Both numbers can be real, honestly reported, and still answer different questions.

items.prompt: As the base rate of an event gets rarer (holding the detector's true/false positive rates fixed), what generally happens to precision?
choices: It generally decreases -- rarer events mean a smaller pool of real cases relative to the huge pool of non-events generating false alarms
It generally increases, since rarer events are easier to detect confidently
It stays exactly the same regardless of base rate
It becomes impossible to compute
items.explanation: As shown by the mermaid loop and the worked table, a rarer base rate shrinks the true-positive pool relative to the ever-large non-event pool generating false alarms, generally pulling precision down.
items.reference:
🧮 base rate fallacy: ignoring how rare the event is
🔀 confusing true positive rate with precision

Why: Both numbers can be real, honestly reported, and still answer different questions.

items.prompt: According to L2, what's the shared fix for both correlation-vs-causation traps and the base rate fallacy?
choices: Stop trusting the summary number, and ask what it's actually built from
Always collect a bigger sample size before drawing any conclusion
Never trust any detector or correlation, ever
Wait for a second, independent data source before acting on any single number
items.explanation: L2's closing point is that a correlation coefficient and an 'accuracy' percentage both hide the details that actually matter -- the fix is investigating what's underneath the summary number in each case.
items.reference:
🔍 correlation coefficient hides mechanism, direction, third causes
🔍 accuracy % hides how rare the event actually is

Why: Both traps involve a rigorous-looking number substituting for a harder investigation underneath it.

items.prompt: Why does a correlation coefficient alone fail to distinguish a confound from a real causal relationship?
choices: Because the coefficient only measures how closely two quantities move together, with no information about mechanism or which variable, if either, is driving the other
Because correlation coefficients are only valid for causal relationships in the first place
Because a confound always produces a negative correlation coefficient
Because correlation coefficients can't be computed when a confound is present
items.explanation: A correlation coefficient is purely a measure of how closely two series move together -- it carries no information about why, so a confound-driven correlation and a genuinely causal one look identical as a number.
items.reference:
🔍 correlation coefficient hides mechanism, direction, third causes
🔍 accuracy % hides how rare the event actually is

Why: Both traps involve a rigorous-looking number substituting for a harder investigation underneath it.

items.prompt: In L3's synthetic-data code, generateData() never writes a line connecting errorRate directly to ticketVolume. Yet pearsonCorrelation(errorRate, ticketVolume) returns about 0.65. Why?
choices: Because both errorRate and ticketVolume are independently computed from the shared variable traffic, so they move together whenever traffic does
Because pearsonCorrelation() has a bug that inflates the result
Because the gaussian() noise function secretly links the two series
Because 200 samples is too few for the correlation to be meaningful
items.explanation: Both series are built as (coefficient) * traffic + independent noise -- whenever the synthetic traffic value is high or low in a given sample, both derived series tend to follow, producing a real correlation with zero direct connection between them.
items.reference:
📈 naive r(errorRate, ticketVolume) ≈ 0.65
🎛️ partial r, controlling for traffic ≈ 0.01

Why: The confound is made literal in code -- the correlation exists entirely through the shared variable, never a direct link.

items.prompt: What does pearsonCorrelation(xs, ys) returning a value close to 1 (versus close to 0) indicate about xs and ys?
choices: A value close to 1 means xs and ys move together very closely (linearly); close to 0 means little to no linear relationship
A value close to 1 means xs causes ys directly
A value close to 0 means the two arrays must be the same length
A value close to 1 means the two arrays share no common cause
items.explanation: Pearson correlation measures the strength of a linear relationship between two series -- values near 1 (or -1) indicate a strong relationship, near 0 a weak one. It says nothing about cause on its own.
items.reference:
📈 naive r(errorRate, ticketVolume) ≈ 0.65
🎛️ partial r, controlling for traffic ≈ 0.01

Why: The confound is made literal in code -- the correlation exists entirely through the shared variable, never a direct link.

items.prompt: What does partialCorrelation(rXY, rXZ, rYZ) compute, conceptually?
choices: The correlation between X and Y with the shared influence of Z algebraically subtracted out
The average of the three input correlations
The correlation between Z and both X and Y combined
Whether X causes Y, as a true/false answer
items.explanation: Partial correlation estimates what the X-Y correlation would look like if Z were held constant -- exactly the 'controlling for the confound' step L2 described, done algebraically instead of by literally holding Z fixed.
items.reference:
🎛️ partial correlation: X vs Y, with Z's shared effect removed
0️⃣ result near 0 means the confound explains the whole correlation

Why: This is the code-level version of 'does the relationship survive once the shared cause is held constant.'

items.prompt: In L3, the partial correlation between errorRate and ticketVolume (controlling for traffic) comes out to about 0.01, versus a naive correlation of about 0.65. What does that near-zero result mean?
choices: Once traffic's shared influence is removed, essentially none of the original correlation remains -- traffic fully explains the relationship
The two variables are now proven to have no relationship in any circumstance
The partial correlation calculation must have an error, since it dropped so much
Traffic and errorRate are unrelated to each other
items.explanation: A partial correlation near zero means the original correlation was almost entirely attributable to the shared confound -- exactly what the synthetic data was constructed to demonstrate.
items.reference:
🎛️ partial correlation: X vs Y, with Z's shared effect removed
0️⃣ result near 0 means the confound explains the whole correlation

Why: This is the code-level version of 'does the relationship survive once the shared cause is held constant.'

items.prompt: L3 shows a detector improved to 99% true positive rate and 1% false positive rate, applied to a rarer 0.1% base rate event, has WORSE precision (about 9%) than L1's original 95%/5% detector at a 2% base rate (28%). Why?
choices: The base rate got ten times rarer at the same time the detector improved, and that base-rate effect dominated the improvement
The alertPrecision() function has a bug that ignores true positive rate improvements
A 99% true positive rate is actually mathematically impossible to achieve
False positive rate improvements never affect precision, only true positive rate does
items.explanation: Even with both error rates improved, the ten-times-rarer base rate shrank the real-event pool so much that false alarms from the enormous non-event pool still dominate -- a 'better' detector on a rarer event can still end up less trustworthy.
items.reference:
🚨 95%/5% detector, 2% base rate → 28% precision
🔎 99%/1% detector, 0.1% base rate → 9% precision

Why: A rarer base rate can overwhelm a genuinely better detector's improvement.

items.prompt: For a very rare event (very low base rate), which improvement to a detector generally moves precision more: raising the true positive rate, or lowering the false positive rate?
choices: Lowering the false positive rate, since it applies to the dominant (much larger) pool of non-events
Raising the true positive rate, since it's the detector's headline 'accuracy' number
Both move precision by exactly the same amount, always
Neither one affects precision when the base rate is very low
items.explanation: At a low base rate, the non-event pool is enormous relative to the real-event pool, so the false positive rate (applied to that huge pool) has outsized leverage over precision compared to the true positive rate.
items.reference:
🚨 95%/5% detector, 2% base rate → 28% precision
🔎 99%/1% detector, 0.1% base rate → 9% precision

Why: A rarer base rate can overwhelm a genuinely better detector's improvement.

items.prompt: L3 lists three proxies for causal reasoning when a true controlled experiment isn't possible. Which of these is one of them?
choices: A natural experiment -- a real-world event that changes one variable without the researcher's involvement
Increasing the correlation coefficient's decimal precision
Running the same correlation calculation twice to confirm it
Renaming the confound so it no longer appears in the analysis
items.explanation: Natural experiments, before/after with a control group, and mechanism plausibility are the three proxies L3 names -- each weaker than a true randomized experiment but stronger than a raw correlation.
items.reference:
🌪️ natural experiment: an unplanned real-world shift
📊 before/after with a control group
🧭 mechanism plausibility

Why: None of these is as strong as a true randomized experiment, but each is stronger than a raw correlation alone.

items.prompt: Why does randomly assigning users to a treatment and control group (a true controlled experiment) rule out confounds that weren't even named in advance?
choices: Random assignment balances every confound, known or unknown, across both groups on average -- not just the ones a researcher thought to measure
It doesn't -- a controlled experiment only rules out confounds the researcher explicitly lists beforehand
Because random assignment always guarantees a large enough sample size
Because randomization removes the need to measure the outcome variable at all
items.explanation: Randomization's power is that it balances ALL potential confounds across groups by construction, including ones nobody thought to name -- unlike a partial correlation, which only controls for the confounds explicitly included in the calculation.
items.reference:
🌪️ natural experiment: an unplanned real-world shift
📊 before/after with a control group
🧭 mechanism plausibility

Why: None of these is as strong as a true randomized experiment, but each is stronger than a raw correlation alone.

items.prompt: A partial correlation controlling for one known confound comes back near zero. Does this prove the relationship is definitely not causal in any way?
choices: No -- it only rules out the specific confound that was controlled for; an unmeasured confound could still exist
Yes -- a partial correlation near zero always proves no causal relationship exists
Yes, but only if the sample size was above 1,000
No -- partial correlation can never meaningfully test for a confound
items.explanation: Partial correlation only removes the influence of the specific variable it's given -- it says nothing about confounds nobody thought to measure and include, which is exactly why L3 frames it as weaker than a true randomized experiment.
items.reference:
🎛️ partial correlation only controls for named confounds
🎲 a true random experiment controls for all confounds, named or not

Why: 'Controlled for one confound' is not the same claim as 'proven causal.'

items.prompt: Why is mechanism plausibility (can anyone describe how A would cause B?) listed as a proxy for causal reasoning, weaker than a controlled experiment but still useful?
choices: Because a strong correlation with no describable mechanism in either direction is a real signal the relationship may be coincidental, even without a formal test
Because mechanism plausibility mathematically proves causation once a mechanism is described
Because it's exactly as strong as a randomized controlled trial
Because it replaces the need to compute any correlation at all
items.explanation: A plausible, describable mechanism doesn't prove causation, but its total absence is a real warning sign -- it's a useful, low-cost sanity check even though it's weaker evidence than an actual controlled comparison.
items.reference:
🎛️ partial correlation only controls for named confounds
🎲 a true random experiment controls for all confounds, named or not

Why: 'Controlled for one confound' is not the same claim as 'proven causal.'

items.prompt: Complete alertPrecision({ baseRate, truePositiveRate, falsePositiveRate }), returning the probability the event is real given the alert fired -- exactly L3's calculator.

tests.description: L1's numbers (2% base rate, 95% TPR, 5% FPR) give about 27.9% precision
a rare 0.1% base rate with a 99%/1% detector gives about 9% precision

items.explanation: This is Bayes' theorem for a binary signal: the numerator is the probability of a real event AND the alert firing, and the denominator is the total probability the alert fires at all (real-and-fired plus not-real-and-fired). Dividing gives precision -- the base rate fallacy made concrete and checkable.
items.reference:
🧮 numerator: baseRate × truePositiveRate
➗ denominator: numerator + (1 - baseRate) × falsePositiveRate

items.prompt: Same alertPrecision(). Confirm it handles a base rate of 0 (event never happens) and a base rate of 1 (event always happens).

tests.description: a base rate of 0 means any alert that fires is always a false alarm, giving 0 precision (as long as falsePositiveRate > 0)
a base rate of 1 means every check is a real event, giving 100% precision regardless of the false positive rate

items.explanation: At baseRate 0, pAlertAndReal is 0 and the entire denominator comes from false positives, so precision is 0. At baseRate 1, (1 - baseRate) is 0, so pAlertAndNotReal vanishes and precision reduces to pAlertAndReal / pAlertAndReal = 1 -- the false positive rate becomes irrelevant once every check is a real event.
items.reference:
🧮 numerator: baseRate × truePositiveRate
➗ denominator: numerator + (1 - baseRate) × falsePositiveRate

Why: This is Bayes' theorem written as plain arithmetic on the real counts from L1/L2's table.

items.prompt: Complete pearsonCorrelation(xs, ys), returning the Pearson correlation coefficient between two equal-length arrays of numbers -- exactly L3's correlation function.

tests.description: two perfectly linearly related arrays (y = 2x) have a correlation of 1
two perfectly inversely related arrays (y = -2x) have a correlation of -1

items.explanation: This centers both arrays around their means, sums the products of the deviations (the covariance-like numerator), and normalizes by the geometric mean of each array's own sum of squared deviations -- exactly L3's implementation, which is why perfectly linear data returns exactly 1 or -1.

➗ normalize the summed products by each array's own spread

Why: This is the standard Pearson formula, applied directly -- the same function L3 runs against the synthetic error-rate/ticket-volume data.

two arrays with a real but weaker linear trend still compute correctly

items.explanation: When ys never varies, sumSqY is 0, making the denominator 0 and the result NaN rather than a defined correlation -- a real edge case worth knowing about before trusting an automated pipeline that computes correlations over many variable pairs, some of which might be constant.
